english: Will you trade me your goat for my dog? -- Your dog, is it good? -- It is good. It quickly guards the sheep from wolves. -- Then what do you want from me for the goat? -- My dog eats meat, and I would milk your goat. -- The (he-)goat gives me no milk and devours grass. -- Then I don't want it. I don't want your dog. -- We laugh.
uncertain: kʷíd káprom lubʰyési: 'what' vs yes/no particle
h₂ml̥ǵyéh₁m̥ read as 1sg optative 'I would milk'

english: Friend, I have driven my wagon here to you. The wheel broke against a post. -- It is my wagon (?). My grandfather built one wheel for me. -- I don't want that. I will make you a new wheel. -- Don't you build wheels? -- Now I give you two rams. -- That is a fair word. Drive the rams to my field.

Look at the cow I drove home here yesterday in winter. It is my cow. A thief drove it from the pasture by night. -- I did not know that; I bought it for three sheep. -- Who sold it to you? -- A stranger sold it; he had a black horse. -- He is the thief. Give me my cow and take two sheep. -- That is right. May the gods see the thief.
uncertain: h₁ésmey h₁ést as dative of possession

english: Wife, I have silver. -- What is silver? I don't know it. -- It is white and kings like it. -- Does it yield milk? -- It yields no milk; with it you buy cows. -- Silver is worth ?? to you, and I do not sell the cattle. Now I will buy wool from you with the silver. -- I will sell you wool; my daughter weaves beautifully.
uncertain: góleti unknown verb (perhaps 'is worth little / is a lack')

english: O Good-fame, I come home (to you). I give you this cup. -- It is beautiful. Where did you find it? -- My brother bought it for two rams. -- Don't go away! Take this garment; my lady wove it. -- Giver, may the gods give you good things. -- Health to the guest; be well, and come again in spring.

Hundred-fame, I owe you three sheep. I bring you six lambs here. -- Would you exchange six lambs for three sheep? -- Lambs will become sheep. -- And who will feed them in winter? -- I give you six loads of grain. -- Now drive the lambs into my cow-pen. Now you owe me nothing. May the gods protect you and the sheep.
